reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: Monitoring Framework: Delivery Methods, Items to Monitor, Plans Review, and Inspector Tools
sections.summary: Inspector is the 'eyes and ears' of the owner — more than a blow counter. DBB: inspector reviews plan, approves hammer, makes driving decisions, produces driving criteria. DB: inspector observes DB-team work and communicates concerns; all decisions made by DB team. Inspector must know: who to contact, whom to send records, what reports are required, and how to notify contractor of deviations without directing their work. Inspector tools listed in Figure 18-2; plans/specs review is the first task before any driving begins.
sections.body:
Construction monitoring and inspection play a critical role in proper pile installation. The trend toward fewer piles with higher nominal resistance increases the importance of monitoring due to less redundancy, smaller tolerances, and higher resistance factors.

The inspector is the 'eyes and ears' for the owner and engineer — not merely a 'blow counter'. Timely observations, suggestions, reporting, and correction advice can ultimately reduce total project cost. The inspector must understand hammer operation, pile behavior, soil conditions, and their interactions.

18.1 MONITORING NEEDS BASED ON THE PROJECT DELIVERY METHOD

Design-Bid-Build (DBB): Agency inspector reviews pile installation plan, approves or reviews hammer submittal and analyses, inspects and records test pile driving, performs resistance verification observations, analyzes results, establishes driving criteria, determines order lengths, inspects production piles, and certifies foundation.

Design-Build (DB): DB team submits plan; agency inspector observes DB-team installation and documentation, communicates concerns to engineer, checks that piles met driving criteria, and reviews DB-team driving criteria. CMGC contracts may follow either DBB or DB duties depending on the project.

Table 18-1 provides a side-by-side comparison of inspection duties for DBB vs. DB delivery.

18.2 ITEMS TO BE MONITORED

Regardless of delivery method, monitoring items include test piles (for order lengths and load testing) and production piles. Key monitoring items: pile installation plan and hammer submittal; test pile installation; nominal resistance verification; driving criteria and production pile order lengths; production pile installation; foundation certification.

18.3 REVIEW OF PROJECT PLANS AND SPECIFICATIONS

First task in monitoring: thoroughly review project plans and specs for pile foundations. All equipment, procedures, and test programs should be clearly understood. Inspector must understand their organizational role (observational or decision-making) and know: whom to contact if problems arise; whom to send driving records and reports; what reports are required; how to notify contractor of deviations without directing their work.

18.4 INSPECTOR'S TOOLS

Figure 18-2 (after Williams Earth Science 1995) lists tools the pile inspector should have available. Inspector should be familiar with proper operation of all hammers on site and may contact hammer manufacturer for additional information. Operating characteristics for all hammer types are provided in Chapter 15.

sections.title: Inspection of Piles Prior to and During Installation
sections.summary: Certificate of compliance required for all pile types. Timber: check species, length/butt/toe size, grain, straightness, treatment, banding, shoes, and splices. Concrete: casting-yard inspection (forms, reinforcement, prestress, splice or toe protection details, concrete strength, handling) plus site inspection (length/section, no shipping damage, proper storage, correct lifting, no splicing after casting when avoidable). H-piles: grade/length/section, shoes, splices (full penetration or proprietary), flange orientation (bending stronger perpendicular to flanges). Pipe piles: grade/length/section, closed-end closure plate or open-end cutting shoe, splice, no internal damage.
sections.body:
A certificate of compliance for the piles is generally required by specifications. The inspector should obtain this certificate and compare specification requirements with the information provided.

18.5.1 Timber Piles (ASTM D25)
- Specified species; minimum length with correct toe and butt sizes; butt cut squarely.
- Acceptable twist of spiral grain and knot distribution.
- Acceptably straight.
- Pressure treated as specified.
- Pile butts and/or toe banded as required (Chapter 16).
- Steel shoes properly attached (Chapter 16).
- Splices (if allowed) meet project requirements.

18.5.2 Precast Concrete Piles
Casting yard inspection (when applicable): form geometry; dimensions/quantity/quality of spiral reinforcing and prestressing steel strands; splice or toe protection connection details; concrete mix design, batching, and placement; prestressing forces, procedures, and tension release timing; handling/storage procedures and minimum curing time.

Site inspection: specified length and section; many specifications require minimum wait after casting before driving or require minimum concrete strength. No evidence of shipping damage. Piles stored above ground on adequate blocking. Piles lifted properly with slings at correct pick-up points — chain slings should not be used. Inspect for cracks or spalling.

18.5.3 Steel H-Piles
- Specified steel grade, length, or section/weight.
- Pile shoes as specified (Chapter 16).
- Splices: proprietary or full penetration groove welds, top and bottom sections in good alignment before splicing (Chapter 16).
- Pile splices and toe attachments properly welded.
- Correct flange orientation per plans — H-pile bending resistance is considerably greater perpendicular to flanges.
- No observable pile damage, including deformations at pile head.

18.5.4 Steel Pipe Piles
- Specified steel grade, length, and minimum section/weight (wall thickness); seamless or spiral welded as specified.
- Driven open or closed end. Closed-end: correct closure plate/conical point size (diameter and thickness) properly welded. Open-end: cutting shoes properly welded.
- Splices meet specifications.
- No observable pile damage, including deformations at pile head.
- After installation: closed-end pipes visually inspected for damage or water prior to concrete filling.
key_points: Certificate of compliance required for all pile types — compare against specification requirements
Timber: verify species, banding, shoes, pressure treatment; splices only if specified
Concrete: casting-yard inspection includes prestress, splice/toe details, mix and curing; minimum wait period or concrete strength before driving
Concrete: inspect for cracks/spalling from shipping; proper storage on blocking; chain slings not permitted for lifting
H-pile: correct flange orientation is critical — bending resistance significantly greater perpendicular to flanges
H-pile: full penetration groove welds or approved proprietary splices with sections in good alignment before welding
Pipe pile (closed-end): inspect for water or damage inside pile before concrete filling

sections.title: Inspection of Driving Equipment Before and During Installation
sections.summary: 18.6 (pre-driving): Hammer cushion must fit snugly in helmet; replace before >50% compression or charring; wood pile cushions last ~1,000-2,000 blows; min. 4 inch pile cushion for concrete; first 100 blows after cushion replacement invalid for blow count. Predrilling/jetting depth must not exceed allowable limits. 18.7 (during driving): Per-hammer checklists and inspection forms. Single acting diesel stroke from Eq. 18-1 (bpm). Double acting diesel: record bounce chamber pressure at EOD/restrike. Pre-ignition inflates blow count — investigate with dynamic testing. Tables 18-2 through 18-6: common problems and indicators by hammer type.
sections.body:
18.6 INSPECTION OF DRIVING EQUIPMENT (before driving)

Pre-driving checklist:
1. Hammer should be approved make/model meeting specification requirements. For adjustable stroke hammers, confirm the stroke necessary for required energy can be obtained.
2. Hammer cushion: correct material type, size, and thickness — must fit snugly inside helmet. Incorrect diameter causes cushion to break or deform. Some air/steam hammers require specific total cushion + striker plate thickness for valve timing. Check before driving and periodically during production. Replace if excessively compressed, burned, or charred.
3. Helmet (drive cap): should fit the pile head securely and allow proper alignment.
4. Pile cushion (concrete piles): required thickness from wave equation analysis but not less than 4 inches. New plywood, hardwood, or composite wood — not water soaked — for every pile. Replace before >50% compression, burning, or charring. Wood cushions deteriorate after ~1,000-2,000 blows. Do not use blow counts obtained during first 100 blows after pile cushion replacement for nominal resistance verification — new cushions reduce energy transfer and inflate blow count.
5. Predrilling/jetting/spudding: depth must not exceed allowable limits. Exceeding allowed depth reduces nominal resistance and may make pile acceptance questionable.
6. Lead system: hold hammer and pile in alignment. Poor alignment reduces energy transfer and increases pile bending and contact stresses. A pile gate at lead bottom that properly centers the pile should be required.

18.7 INSPECTION OF DRIVING EQUIPMENT DURING INSTALLATION

Two supposedly identical hammers (same make/model) may not drive alike due to friction losses, valve timing, air supply hose condition, fuel type, and maintenance status. Inspector should become familiar with proper operation of each hammer.

18.7.1 Drop Hammers: Confirm ram weight (calculated from volume × 492 lb/ft³ if needed). Leads must allow ram to fall without obstruction. Hammer hoist line always slack.

18.7.2 Single Acting Air/Steam Hammers: Confirm ram weight. Check air/steam supply pressure and flow (pressure at compressor = rated pressure + hose losses; should not vary during driving). Check slide bar and cams for wear, lubrication. Verify stroke meets specification (observe directly). Slower bpm implies reduced stroke from inadequate pressure/volume, restricted hose, or improper lubrication. As blow count increases, stroke may increase causing racking — reduce flow until racking stops. Hammers may void warranty above 10 blows/inch beyond short periods. Common problems: Table 18-2. Inspector form: Figure 18-8.

18.7.3 Double Acting or Differential Air/Steam Hammers: Similar to single acting but ~half the rated energy comes from pressure on ram during downstroke. Reducing pressure flow to prevent racking also reduces energy. Common problems: Table 18-2. Inspector form: Figure 18-9.

18.7.4 Single Acting Diesel Hammers: Check exhaust ports open, recoil dampener condition and thickness. Ram stroke determined by saximeter (time between blows) or computed from Equation 18-1 (stroke h in feet from bpm). Watch for pre-ignition — fuel burns before impact, less energy to pile, inflated blow count. If piles driven with cold hammer drive deeper, or blow count decreases after short breaks, investigate pre-ignition with dynamic testing. Low strokes from poor compression (worn/defective piston or anvil rings). Common problems: Table 18-3. Inspector form: Figure 18-12.

18.7.5 Double Acting Diesel Hammers: Always measure bounce chamber pressure, especially at EOD or restrike — indirectly measures equivalent stroke or energy. Manufacturer supplies chart relating bounce chamber pressure to rated energy. Bounce chamber pressure requires correction for batter piles. Pre-ignition concern same as single acting. Common problems: Table 18-4. Inspector form: Figure 18-14.

18.7.6 Single Acting Hydraulic Hammers: Check hydraulic power supply pressure, flow, and hose condition. Hydraulic hammers must be kept clean and free of dirt and water. Warm up before operation; do not shut down immediately after driving. For observable-ram models, stroke can be observed directly or via sensors. Common problems: Table 18-5. Inspector form: Figure 18-15.

18.7.7 Double Acting Hydraulic Hammers: Most have built-in sensors to determine ram velocity at impact; result converted to kinetic energy. Most are steel-on-steel (no hammer cushion); models for concrete piles have synthetic anvil. Check and record pre-charge pressures or accumulators. Common problems: Table 18-6. Inspector form: Figure 18-17.

18.7.8 Resonant Hammers: Confirm make/model, check hydraulic power supply, record resonant vibrating frequency, check hydraulic clamps for attachment to pile.

18.7.9 Vibratory Hammers: Confirm make/model, check hydraulic power supply, record vibrating frequency if available, check hydraulic clamps. Hoist line slack for installation; tight for extraction. Leads rarely used.

sections.title: Inspection of Test/Indicator Piles and Production Piles
sections.summary: 18.8: Preconstruction meeting to clarify 13 decision authorities before test pile driving. 18.9: 17-item per-pile checklist. Displacement pile group sequence: center outward — NOT outside-to-center (trapped soil prevents center piles reaching min. penetration). Drive piles nearest adjacent structures first. Vibration settlement damage in loose sands possible up to 1,300 ft; preconstruction survey within 400 ft. Blow counts >10 blows/inch avoided by proper pile/hammer matching. Table 18-7: common installation problems (refusal, deeper driving, abrupt blow count change, misalignment, concrete cracking) and solutions.
sections.body:
18.8 INSPECTION OF TEST OR INDICATOR PILES

Test piles provide the basis for adjusting driving criteria before production pile installation begins. On smaller projects, a single static or dynamic test pile may suffice; on larger projects, multiple test piles distributed across the site are used to verify or adjust criteria as conditions vary.

A preconstruction pile driving meeting between contractor, project administrator, and inspector is often beneficial to clarify the following 13 decision authorities before test pile driving:
1. Who determines test pile locations?
2. Who determines test pile driving criteria?
3. Who stops driving when criterion is met?
4. Who decides at what depth to stop indicator/test piles?
5. Who checks cutoff elevations?
6. Who checks for heave?
7. Who determines if static/dynamic test results indicate acceptable test pile?
8. Who determines if additional tests are required?
9. Who determines if modifications to procedures or equipment are required?
10. What documentation is required and who produces what?
11. Who produces production pile driving criteria and how quickly will it be available?
12. Who has authority to allow production pile installation to begin?
13. When is authorization to proceed given relative to test pile analysis?

Partinent observations must be reported quickly for immediate corrective action. Dynamic tests assess hammer performance and driving stresses during initial driving, and nominal resistance during restrike.

18.9 INSPECTION OF PRODUCTION PILES

17-item per-pile checklist (checks for each pile):
1. Correct type, size, length, and strength?
2. Correct location within acceptable tolerances and correct orientation?
3. Splices made to specification?
4. Pile toe protection required and properly attached?
5. Pile acceptably plumb?
6. Hammer working correctly?
7. Hammer cushion correct type and thickness?
8. Pile cushion correct type and thickness (concrete piles)?
9. [Additional checklist items from specifications...]
14. Pipe piles visually inspected before concrete filling; correct concrete strength; samples taken?
15. Piles to be filled with concrete cleaned properly after driving?
16. Pile integrity issues resolved?
17. Documentation complete and submitted timely?

Cushion replacement: do not use blow counts from first 100 blows after pile cushion replacement — new cushions reduce energy transfer and inflate blow count.

Driving stresses: keep within specified limits. If dynamic testing not used, wave equation analysis essential to evaluate anticipated driving stresses. Driving at blow counts above 10 blows/inch should be avoided by proper pile/hammer matching.

Displacement pile group driving sequence: drive center-outward or row-by-row from one side. Do NOT drive from outside inward — displaced soil trapped and compacted in center prevents center piles from reaching minimum penetration depths, particularly for scour.

Driving near existing structures: drive piles nearest the structure first, work away. Soil displacement toward adjacent structures can cause problems; can be especially critical near bascule bridges where small movements prevent locking mechanisms.

Vibrations: damage relatively uncommon within one pile length of driving. Settlement damage from vibration-induced compaction of loose clean sands possible up to 1,300 feet from driving. Preconstruction survey of structures and utilities within 400 feet of pile driving activities often required.

Table 18-7 provides common pile installation problems and solutions, including: piles encountering refusal above minimum penetration (check drivability, dynamic measurements), piles driving significantly deeper than estimated (wave equation analysis and restrike), abrupt decrease in blow count (pile toe damage likely), blow count lower than expected (pile damage below grade), piles driving out of alignment/location tolerance (pile gate or template), obstructions at depth, concrete pile cracking in easy or hard driving, and steel/timber head deformation.

sections.title: Driving Records, Reports, and Safety
sections.summary: Driving records are the basis for payment, engineering decisions, and litigation. Required items: date, project/structure/pile ID, weather, contractor, hammer (make/model/ram/energy/stroke/speed), hammer cushion, pile cushion (depth changed), pile (location/type/size/length), elevations (ground/cutoff/final), blow count (blows/ft; final 1 ft in blows/inch), comments, and inspector signature. Safety: 100-ft pile can fall 100 ft during positioning — plan escape route; concrete/timber piles can break suddenly; steel piles can buckle; avoid area beneath suspended loads and behind crane.
sections.body:
18.10 DRIVING RECORDS AND REPORTS

Pile driving records vary by organization. Minimum required data for each pile (Figure 18-19 shows typical pile driving log):
1. Date.
2. Project name, structure number, substructure unit, and pile number/designation.
3. Project location.
4. Weather and temperature conditions.
5. Name of the contractor.
6. Hammer make, model, ram weight, and energy rating. Record actual stroke and operating speed whenever changed.
7. Hammer cushion description, size and thickness, and helmet weight.
8. Pile cushion description, size and thickness; depth where changed.
9. Pile location, type, size, and length.
10. Pile number or designation matching pile layout plans.
11. Pile ground surface, cutoff, and final penetration elevations and embedded length.
12. Penetration resistance data in blows per foot with final 1 foot recorded in blows per inch.
13. Graphical presentation of driving data (optional).
14. Cutoff length, length in ground, and order length.
15. Comments or unusual observations, including reasons for all interruptions.
16. Signature and title of inspector.

Importance of detailed records: basis for payment and engineering decisions regarding foundation adequacy. Great importance in litigations involving claims. Sloppy, inaccurate, or incomplete records encourage claims and result in higher cost foundations. Better documentation → lower foundation cost → more successful projects.

A daily inspection report (Figure 18-20) is also prepared summarizing all driving activities during the day.

18.11 SAFETY

Pile driving involves heavy equipment and heavy loads. Key safety considerations:
- Pile positioning is one of the most dangerous operations: a 100-foot pile can fall 100 feet from the pile location during positioning. Plan escape route before pile lifting and positioning begins.
- Avoid area beneath suspended loads — hoisting device failure can cause serious injury.
- Avoid area behind crane; be aware when crane is moving or swinging.
- Maintain sufficient distance from pile location during driving — position to avoid area immediately in front of pile.
- Heavy pieces can fall from hammer or helmet during operation.
- Concrete and timber piles can break suddenly; long steel piles can buckle — make area around pile location dangerous.
- Inspector must also avoid positioning below or near the hammer.
